$comment: Teaching content for cl_mcp — MCP as seen from the Messages API. Server-building lives in section 6.

knowledgePoints.name: Your stuff, your processes, everyone else's stuff
knowledgePoints.teach:
connects Claude towho maintains it
Toolsyour systems — your database, your APIsyou own the code and the maintenance
Skillsa procedure — your report template, your checklistyou, but they are instructions, not integrations
MCPthird-party servicesthe provider maintains the integration

Tools are for your stuff, skills are for your processes, MCP is for everyone else's stuff.

The maintenance column is the one that decides most real cases. Writing a Slack tool yourself means owning its schema, its auth, and its breakage every time Slack changes something — which is precisely the work an MCP server exists to absorb.

questions.q: Claude must follow your firm's report template, query your internal database, and read Slack. Which mechanism for each?
options: Tool, skill, MCP
MCP, tool, skill
Skill, tool, MCP
Skill, MCP, tool
questions.explain: Template is a procedure (skill), your database is your system (tool), Slack is third-party (MCP).

questions.q: What is the practical argument for MCP over writing the tool yourself?
options: MCP tools run noticeably faster than yours
The provider maintains the schema and auth
MCP tools do not consume any of your context
MCP tools can be called without any loop
questions.explain: Maintenance moves to whoever owns the service.

reviewQuestions.q: A skill is best described as…
options: An integration with an external service
A tool whose schema gets auto-generated
A server-side tool that Anthropic runs
Instructions teaching Claude a procedure
reviewQuestions.explain: Procedure, not plumbing — your template or checklist expressed as instructions.

knowledgePoints.name: Two fields, and a schema you never write
knowledgePoints.teach:
Connecting a remote MCP server takes two pieces in the request.

1. Declare the connection — mcp_servers:

"mcp_servers": [{
  "type": "url",
  "url":  "https://mcp.example.com/slack",
  "name": "slack",
  "authorization_token": "..."      # optional
}]

2. Grant access — a tool entry pointing at it:

"tools": [{"type": "mcp_toolset", "mcp_server_name": "slack"}]

Default is all tools on that server.

Claude introspects the server and discovers the tools and schemas itself. You never write a tool schema by hand for an MCP-provided tool.

(As of the course, the MCP connector required a beta header.)

questions.q: Which two request fields connect a remote MCP server?
options: mcp_servers, plus a tools mcp_toolset entry
mcp_servers and mcp_tools on the request
servers and tool_choice, on the request
mcp_config and allowed_tools, together
questions.explain: One declares the connection, the other grants access to it.

questions.q: Who writes the schemas for MCP-provided tools?
options: You, mirroring the server's documentation
The SDK, from the server's OpenAPI spec
Nobody — Claude introspects the server
Anthropic, from a registry of known servers
questions.explain: Introspection is the point of the protocol. Hand-writing schemas is what MCP removes.

reviewQuestions.q: What does an mcp_toolset entry grant by default?
options: No tools at all until each is enabled
Every tool on the server that is named
Only the read-only tools that it exposes
Only tools whose schemas Claude validates
reviewQuestions.explain: All of them — which is exactly why scoping down is a separate, deliberate step.

knowledgePoints.name: Disable everything, then enable a few
knowledgePoints.teach:
Since the default grants every tool on the server, you invert it:

"default_config": {"enabled": False},
"configs": {
    "search_messages": {"enabled": True},
    "list_channels":   {"enabled": True}
}

Deny by default, then allow by name. A Slack connection becomes read-only: search and list reachable, post and delete not.

Why deny-by-default rather than listing what to block? Because a block list is only correct until the provider adds a tool. The server gains delete_channel in a release you did not read about, and an allow list still does not include it while a block list silently does not exclude it.

And note what this is not: an instruction. Telling the agent in its system prompt never to post is a request that untrusted content in context can argue with. Configuration cannot be argued with.

questions.q: You connect a Slack MCP server and the agent must never post. What do you do?
options: A system-prompt rule forbidding posting
List the posting tools in a blocked set
Use tool_choice to restrict what may run
default_config disabled, then enable reads
questions.explain: Deny by default, allow by name. It is configuration, and it survives the provider adding new tools.

questions.q: Why is a block list worse than an allow list here?
options: A new provider tool is permitted by default
It is simply a more verbose thing to write
Block lists are not supported by the API
Block lists cannot combine with auth tokens
questions.explain: Anything unlisted is allowed, and the list of things to block grows without you.

reviewQuestions.q: Why is scoping configuration rather than a prompt instruction?
options: Prompt instructions cost extra tokens
Instructions are ignored for MCP tools
Configuration is enforced; a prompt is asked
Configuration is cached; instructions are not
reviewQuestions.explain: The same programmatic-enforcement-versus-instruction line that runs through the whole certification.
